---
title: "Calibration"
---

Most reconstruction problems are calibration problems. The fusion weights are
functions of spatial frequency, so if the mapping from detector pixels to
reciprocal space is wrong, the weights are wrong, and the result is a plausible
image that is quietly incorrect. This page is the short list of things to get
right.

## The reciprocal pixel size, `dk`

`dk` is **measured**, not assumed. The bright-field disk has a known angular
radius — the convergence semi-angle you supplied — so fitting its radius in pixels
gives the conversion directly:

$$ dk = \frac{\alpha}{r_{\mathrm{BF}}\,\lambda} $$

with $r_\mathrm{BF}$ the fitted radius in pixels and $\lambda$ the relativistic
electron wavelength. `Dataset4dstem.from_array` runs this fit during construction,
and the named datasets arrive already calibrated.

The fit sweeps a set of intensity thresholds and takes the median radius, which is
what makes it insensitive to where exactly you consider the disk edge to be. It
refuses rather than guesses when the pattern has no compact bright region — a fit
whose radius exceeds 40% of the detector usually means the input was not an
averaged diffraction pattern at all.

```python
dk = dataset.calibrate_reciprocal_from_bright_field()
print(dataset.sampling)   # (dy, dx, dky, dkx)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Counting detectors: pass a hot-pixel threshold

On an event-counting detector a single stuck pixel can dominate the maximum the
threshold sweep is relative to, and the fit then locks onto that one pixel. If your
detector counts, pass `hot_pixel_threshold` and check the fitted radius is
physically sensible before trusting it.
:::

## The scan rotation

The angle between the scan axes and the detector axes has to be right, and nothing
downstream can infer it: the autofocus holds rotation **fixed** while it fits
aberrations. A wrong rotation shows up as a reconstruction that is sharp along one
direction and smeared along the other, or as a fused image with directional
artefacts that no amount of aberration fitting removes.

If you know it from the microscope, set it:

```python
dataset.meta.rotation = 84.0   # degrees
```

If you do not, the centre-of-mass field of the bright-field disk determines it: the
correct rotation is the one that makes that field a gradient — curl-free — because
it is the gradient of the projected potential.

## Detector orientation

Worth checking early, because it is easy to miss and it produces a specific,
recognisable failure. If the detector's axes are flipped relative to the scan, the
parallax shifts come out with the wrong handedness, defocus fits toward zero, and
the aberration fit reports a suspiciously small `C10` regardless of the real
defocus. A defocus that will not move off zero is worth suspecting a flip rather
than a fitting problem.

## The aberration starting guess

The autofocus is a local optimisation. It needs a starting defocus, and it raises
if `meta.aberrations` is all zero rather than descending from nothing:

```python
dataset.meta.aberrations.array[0] = -50.0   # C10, Angstrom; defocus == -C10
dataset.determine_aberrations_(correct_order=2)
```

The sign matters more than the magnitude — an estimate within a factor of two is
plenty, but the wrong sign can settle into a mirror-image solution with inverted
contrast. Through-focus contrast inversion in direct ptychography is physical, not
a bug, so a reconstruction that looks inverted may simply be on the other side of
focus.

## Scan step and upsampling

`scan_step` is the pitch of the scan, in Ångström. The reconstruction is upsampled
relative to it, by default to the factor that brings the output pitch to what the
data can support (`upsample="nyquist"`).

That upsampling is why a scale bar needs the reconstruction's sampling, not the
dataset's:

```python
from scatterem.vis.reconstruction_sampling import reconstruction_sampling

sampling = reconstruction_sampling(dataset, fused)
```

Getting this wrong overstates the bar by the upsample factor — four-fold on the
paper's Fig. 4, which is the difference between a correct figure and a wrong one.

## Sanity checks worth running

- **`dk` is not the placeholder.** If `dataset.sampling[2]` is exactly 1.0, the
  bright-field fit fell back and everything downstream is in detector pixels, not
  inverse Ångström.
- **The reconstruction is finite.** A NaN anywhere usually means a division by a
  zero SSNR, which in turn means an empty channel.
- **The bright-field radius is plausible.** Print it. A radius near the detector
  half-width, or a couple of pixels, both mean the fit found the wrong thing.
- **Both channels look sensible on their own** before you read the fused result.
  Fusion cannot rescue a channel that failed; it will just weight it down and leave
  a band with nothing in it.
